title: LayerZero bridge destinations are a governance-configured allowlist: the relayer picks the chain, never the recipient address
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.2.2.1.2.1.2.13.1.4 builds the LayerZero send parameters and shows what the relayer does and does not control. The function signature (A...13.1.1) accepts `oftAddress`, `amount` and `destinationEndpointId` — but not a recipient. The recipient "is read from `layerZeroRecipients` for that endpoint":

```
SendParam({ dstEid: destinationEndpointId, to: layerZeroRecipients[destinationEndpointId], ... })
```

Cross-chain transfer is the operation where an attacker most wants a free-form destination, because it moves value outside the reach of the origin chain's controls and is irreversible. Making the destination a mapping keyed by endpoint reduces the relayer's choice to selecting among destinations governance has already sanctioned.

The rate limit is keyed to match: A...13.1.2 derives it from `keccak256(abi.encode(LIMIT_LAYERZERO_TRANSFER, oftAddress, destinationEndpointId))`, so each token-and-chain pair gets its own budget rather than sharing one global bridging allowance. Opening a new corridor is a deliberate governance act on both the recipient map and the limit registry.

An unset entry in `layerZeroRecipients` yields the zero address, which is why the rate-limit-zero mandate in A...13.1.2 matters as the primary guard — the recipient map alone fails open in the sense that it would attempt a send to `0` rather than reverting on an unconfigured endpoint.
description: SendParam.to is read from layerZeroRecipients[destinationEndpointId] rather than taken as an argument, so a compromised relayer cannot redirect bridged funds to an arbitrary address.
